text.p: U.S. bank stocks are likely to claw back to the highs seen earlier this year and perhaps surpass them as investors see evidence that higher interest rates are not poison for bank stocks, analysts said.
Robert Albertson, analyst at Goldman, Sachs and Co, expects Citicorp to hit a target in the 140s and Chase Manhattan Corp to hit a target in the 120s in the next nine to 12 months.
Earlier this year Citicorp hit a high of 127-1/8 and Chase Manhattan set a high at 110-1/2.
But the bank stocks started falling as speculation heated up that the Fed would raise interest rates in late March. The Fed in fact raised rates 25 basis points to 5.5 percent.
The weakness continued amid speculation the Fed's move would be followed by a further rise in May and perhaps another in July.

Lately, the stocks have been recovering after banks in general reported earnings up 10 percent or better from a year ago. The stocks have also been getting some help from the decline of the yield on the long treasury bond to below seven percent.

But Albertson said the March increase in short rates came too late in the quarter to convince skeptics that bank earnings are not especially sensitive to rate moves. He said that, in a perverse way, he was hoping for a rate rise in May and perhaps one more to really convince the skeptics.
At an investment management conference Thursday, UBS Securities analyst Thomas Hanley said interest rate sensitivity is far less important than in the past.

For one thing, there have been sharp reductions in the amount of government and tax-exempt bond in bank portfolios. At the same time, fee income is contributing a higher proportion of revenues and loans as a percentage of earning assets are much lower.
As for the economic environment, Hanley said Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan "is the key to the whole thing."
The Fed chairman has been "talking up long rates" keeping the dollar relatively high and keeping short rates in a narrow band.

But Hanley expects the economy to pick up in the second half of 1998 and create conditions that will be harder for the Fed to deal with. For now, he expects bank stocks to continue to bounce back and test the old highs. It is not until 1999 that Hanley sees the economic environment creating conditions where bank stocks are candidates for sale.
Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co analyst George Salem said in a research note this week that his affection for bank stocks has diminished, but he would still overweight the group.

On the positive side, he said share price to earnings multiples are low and earnings per share are expected to rise about 12 percent in 1997 and in 1998. He said assuming the Fed tightens short rates once or at most twice, he believes selected bank stocks will outperform the general market.

Salem said one queston he has concerns the emerging markets. The emerging markets have been major contributors to the earnings growth of large multinational banks in the last several years, but now growth appears to be slowing in Asia, while Latin America shows better prospects.
The only credit quality issue of concern to banks lately is credit cards, with the loss rates rising for more than a year.
Albertson said the loss rates are not out of control, nor are they likely to impact earnings.
Hanley expects credit card loss rates to peak at 7.25 percent in the first quarter of 1998. He said the higher loss rates have been a functon of volume growth, but now the growth rate is being cut.
Salem said his favorite bank stocks are Chase Manhattan, NationsBank Corp, Bank of New York Co Inc and NorWest Corp.
Earier this week, Hanley said his favorite money center bank is Citicorp, while his top pick among the super regionals is NationsBank.
